pamphlet_excerpts: Short History of Fingerprinting: Give A Short History: Galton was able to scientifically prove what Herschel and Faulds already suspected: that fingerprints are permanent and unique to each individual (p. 13).
Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 2: Give A Short History Principle 2: According to Galton's calculations, the odds of two individual fingerprints being the samewere 1 in 64 billion (p. 13).

Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 3: Give A Short History Principle 3: In 1891, Juan Vucetich, an Argentine police official, began the first fingerprint files based on Galton pattern types (p. 13).
Short History of Fingerprinting Principle 4: Give A Short History Principle 4: In 1892, Vucetich made the first criminal fingerprint identification (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 1 (Give A Short History): The classification system was basedon Galton's observations, as revised by Sir Edward Richard Henry (p. 13).

Step 2 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 2 (Give A Short History): In 1903, the New York Stateprison system became the first agency in the United States toregularly use fingerprints to identify criminals (p. 13).
Step 3 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 3 (Give A Short History): The Leavenworth bureau became the first to operate on morethan a local basis (p. 13).

Step 4 (Short History of Fingerprinting): Step 4 (Give A Short History): It gradually began to offer a free fingerprintexchange service among a growing list of participating lawenforcement officers (p. 13).

Counselor You Can Identify Principle 2: Your counselor you can identify Principle 2: Learning to recognize thesegeneral patterns and their subcategories is not hard (p. 18).

step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 1 (Your counselor you can identify): In the loop pattern, the ridges begin on one side of the finger, curve or turn back sharply, and end on the same side (p. 18).
Step 2 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 2 (Your counselor you can identify): The loopmay slope or "lean" toward either the thumb or the little finger (p. 18).

Step 3 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 3 (Your counselor you can identify): If you can identify the two bones in your forearm, theradius and ulna, then you can remember the two subcategoriesof loops (p. 18).

Step 4 (Counselor You Can Identify): Step 4 (Your counselor you can identify): The ridges of a radial loop begin and end on the sameside of the hand as the thumb (or the radius, the bone that is on the inside of the arm) (p. 18).
